articles.title_orig: Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.title_zh: Christiane Amanpour is leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Christiane Amanpour attends Variety's Power of Women in New York on April 5, 2019. (Photo by Evan Agostini/Invision/AP, File)
(AP) -- Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour, who began as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on TV, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades, will be leaving the network after 43 years.
Amanpour, the network’s chief international anchor, will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end it in May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement Monday that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour & Co,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said. She added she would “always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: Always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour did not give a reason for her departure, nor did she specifically mention changes at her network. But her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance . After a yearlong process , Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front, Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and two later recurrences, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”
Amanpour joined CNN as an assistant in Atlanta in 1983. In his own message Monday, CNN's chief executive, Mark Thompson, wrote that at the time, her promise was not universally appreciated. “Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent — or to hold any on-air role at all,” Thompson wrote. “Boy, did she prove him wrong!”
Amanpour became a reporter and an international correspondent seven years later. She earned fame in the early 1990s, covering the Gulf War, conflict in the Middle East and many other hot spots. War reporting is “a sense of mission, it’s a sense of purpose, it’s a sense of being able to tell a story,” she said.
She aimed to bring international news — including complicated stories — to American viewers. “I’ve never believed that things are too complicated to put on American television,” she told The Associated Press in 2023. "I’ve never talked down to an audience. I’ve never believed that they just want to know what’s happening in their backyard.”
Amanpour also noted that her upbringing gave her a unique perspective.
“Because of my upbringing — I’m half-Iranian and half-British — I’ve had the great privilege of being able to see the world from two very distinct perspectives,” she said. “I’ve always spoken out about the need to bridge gaps. I know we can live in a world that’s not 100% tribalized.”
In her remarks Monday, Amanpour thanked her field crews and show teams.
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much,” she wrote, “as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.”

articles.title_zh: Meet the researchers leaving the US because of Trump's funding cuts and politicization of science
articles.content_orig:

Halley Froehlich never expected to leave the United States, where her family lineage stretches back to the 1700s, to pursue her scientific career.
Yet, faced with stalled federal grants and growing uncertainty over the country's research environment, she packed her life into boxes and relocated to Finland alongside her husband and daughter. She now studies how climate change affects edible fish, shellfish, and seaweed at the University of Helsinki .
Her departure reflects a wider trend. When the Trump administration began reshaping the American scientific sector last year by altering the federal grant distribution process and seeking greater political influence over funded projects, foreign academic institutions recognized an opportunity.
Many introduced dedicated schemes designed to entice U.S.-based scholars by offering stable financial support and academic freedom.
A growing number of academics have accepted these international offers. Though comprehensive nationwide data remains difficult to aggregate, university officials, researchers, and professional associations describe the ongoing shift as clear, unprecedented, and concerning.
"You can almost talk to any vice president for research at a university and they will tell you of one or two top faculty that they’ve lost," said Tobin Smith, senior vice president of government relations and public policy for the Association of American Universities.
White House spokesperson Liz Huston said Trump is "ending waste" and is "committed to keeping America the world leader in scientific innovation, and that means funding real science."
Despite those assurances, an April report from the Business for Federal Research Funding Coalition revealed that more than half of U.S. states have lost scientists to recruitment programs in other countries.
Survey data from last March indicated that early-career biomedical scientists were about 20 percentage points less likely to say they wanted to stay in the U.S. "now" than they did six months earlier.
Furthermore, figures from the American Institute of Physics show that physics Ph.D. graduates in 2025 departed the U.S. at the highest rate observed in 30 years.
Institutions in nations such as Canada , France , Belgium , and Finland are publicly advertising their success in drawing scholars from U.S. organizations. For a country that far and away leads the world in Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, and chemistry, researchers view this as a disturbing and surprising development.
"It used to be the shining city on the hill where we all want to go," said Christine Stawitz, now at the University of Birmingham in England . "That reputational loss, I think, is hard to quantify, but also really damaging."
Stawitz stepped down from her job at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration last year to become a research software engineer in the United Kingdom .
She noted that NOAA no longer aligned with her values, particularly after receiving directives to strip websites of references to climate change and diversity, equity and inclusion topics.
She added that the state of American science has become a recurring topic of conversation at international gatherings. " People talk about the U.S. at conferences in the U.K. now like, I don't know what's going on there. It's not good," she said.
For Froehlich, the choice to relocate developed over time. Already concerned by issues surrounding school safety and gun violence in the U.S., she watched as the national research landscape was overturned.
At the University of California, Santa Barbara, grant postponements and cancellations left colleagues struggling and student researchers in tears. Doubts regarding future federal backing for her climate-focused research mounted.
"The cumulative effect of those things ultimately ended up making us really serious about, I don’t think here is our home anymore," said Froehlich.
She ultimately accepted an offer through an initiative by the Research Council of Finland, securing five years of guaranteed funding totaling about $3 million. She moved into a flat by the Baltic Sea in Helsinki and is taking university-sponsored Finnish lessons.
Foreign researchers who were drawn to the U.S. for its reputation as a global leader in science are also seeking different places to do their work.
Married biologists James Letts, who is Canadian, and Maria Maldonado, who is Argentinian, left their academic positions at the University of California, Davis to join Australia 's Monash University. Both earned their doctoral degrees in New York and spent over a decade doing science in the U.S.
Grant-related uncertainty—including laying off a staff scientist while waiting for stalled funding—motivated them to make the move.
"All I want to do is do great science and make discoveries, but I want my work to mean something as well. And the opportunity to do that seemed very difficult in the U.S.," Letts said.
Immigrants have historically won 40 percent of the U.S. science Nobel Prizes. However, Omar Yaghi, a 2025 Nobel Prize winner for chemistry, departed his position at the University of California, Berkeley this year to direct an artificial intelligence lab at China’s Tsinghua University.
The U.S. remains a science powerhouse, full of institutions with robust research communities and well-resourced facilities that attract foreign talent.
Even if every European country threw open its doors, there still would not be enough capacity to accommodate every American scientist. Many researchers are choosing to stay, searching for new sources of funding or pivoting to industry positions.
Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the ongoing erosion of reputation and talent. The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $174 billion in federal grants since the president's second term began, according to tracking data compiled by the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness.
Additionally, a proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget could accord political appointees more control over which future projects are funded, though a resolution approved by Congress has delayed a final decision on the rule until December.
Scientists who have moved away and those remaining in the U.S. are worried about what lies ahead. They warn that the next generation of scientists may face fewer graduate programs, diminished funding, and reduced mentorship—effects that could take a decade or longer for the U.S. scientific enterprise to fully feel.
Major research institutions accepted 15% fewer applicants for fall 2026 doctoral programs compared to last year, according to admissions data collected by the Association of American Universities. One of the impacted students was a mentee of Smith's.
"What is one of my pieces of advice to that young man? Next year, look in Canada," he said.

articles.title_orig: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.title_zh: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.content_orig:
Megan Harmes was 14 when she first tried ketamine.
A decade later, rehab is helping her rebuild her life after bladder issues caused by the drug have left her needing to wear incontinence pads.
The drugs charity Kaleidoscope says it has seen a huge rise in referrals to its detox and rehabilitation facility over the last five years, with two people referred in 2021 compared to 112 so far this year. The majority of clients are aged 18 to 24.
Research is now underway by the University of South Wales into the specific needs of this group, as the harm caused by "chronic, escalating use" of ketamine is far more rapid, over a shorter space of time, than from alcohol or Class A drugs.
Services traditionally designed for older adults are having to adapt to support much younger people, it said, with very different needs, with habits often formed while they were in school.
For 24-year-old Megan, from Flint in north Wales, drug use became more common among her peers during lockdown.
As an aeronautical engineering apprentice, she was suddenly working from home, on full pay, with access to a drug whose price had plummeted.
She said at its worst, she was on it "all day, every day", as according to Megan it helped to suppress symptoms or feelings associated with ADHD and borderline personality disorder.
"I'm very hyperactive now that I'm sober. I haven't been like that since I was 14, it suppressed pretty much everything," she said.
Eventually her ketamine use meant she lost her apprenticeship, causing her to "spiral".
Megan later found work elsewhere, but four years of night shifts further entrenched her use, as she would use ketamine to stay awake through the night even on days off.
For the last two years she has been in agony, unable to stand straight and needing to wear incontinence pads.
"For a 22-year-old wearing pads or nappies, it takes away all dignity," she said.
"Back then I really didn't care whether I lived or died - now I don't want to die.
"I've been in rehab just over four weeks and I'm getting back to my old self."
Megan said she wouldn't know the extent of the damage to her bladder for some time, but she has put on weight and is physically feeling better than when she arrived.
Jo Moore runs the Birchwood rehabilitation facility for Kaleidoscope and said five years ago they had just one referral for inpatient detox from ketamine.
"Since January this year we've seen 112 people come through the door," she said, adding that half their clients are currently being supported for ketamine use.
"It's very, very cheap and very accessible - that's what allows people to use it more frequently and at large amounts at the same time."
The drug is prescribed in healthcare settings as a dissociative anaesthetic, and also used with animals, but was reclassified as a Class B drug in 2014. This means it is illegal to take, carry, make or sell.
Illicit ketamine use among those aged between 16 and 59 in the UK was estimated to be about 264,000 people in 2024-25, with those seeking treatment for ketamine use disorders increasing twelvefold over the course of a decade.
While younger people have driven the rise in its use, Moore said the last year had seen a rise in referrals for adults aged 25 to 34, particularly in Cardiff and south-east Wales.
Dr Darren Quelch, from the University of South Wales, said interviews with service users at Birchwood suggested use started from as young as 13.
He said the physical harm caused by persistent use ranged from memory problems and chronic pain to bladder damage and kidney failure, but that support services were having to rapidly adapt as the needs of users are more complex.
"Their bread and butter isn't dealing with really complex medical presentations," he said. "Even if they were, we actually don't know what the right answer is yet."
He is now conducting research alongside Kaleidoscope to establish what types of support work for this specific patient group.
"The population is inherently different to lots of other groups that might engage with drug and alcohol treatment services," he said.
Mark said his health had deteriorated to such an extent that "at the age of 25 I probably had the body of an 80-year-old".
"I was no longer functioning like a proper human being," he said.
As a keen footballer growing up in Liverpool, he now looks on jealously at others his age, walking without pain.
"It stopped me being a father to the little girl that I've got - I stopped being the big brother, the responsible son," he said.
Mark would regularly pass clots and experience pain during urination, but said the collapse of his nose from snorting drugs has had a huge impact.
"It completely destroys self-confidence - which leads to more drugs, because that just blanked out what I think of myself."
It's one of the reasons he has asked to remain anonymous.
"I started getting looks of disgust from my own family, which destroyed me. It was a very lonely time through my addiction," he said.
Mark's drug use started at 18, but by 21 he said he was using "copious amounts of cocaine and ketamine".
He initially sought help from his GP in Liverpool, but was too ashamed to admit he was using ketamine for fear of being dismissed or judged.
"It's a hard lesson learned," he said.
It's an issue reflected in Quelch's research. He found young people struggled with A&E and GP surgeries, as their symptoms weren't always linked with ketamine use, or the question wasn't always asked.
"That's not necessarily because people aren't asking the right question, but we don't actually know what works well at the moment," he said.
"There's very little provision for young people experiencing drug and alcohol-related harms, and that has almost left us starting right from the beginning."
Moore said things were improving, with greater availability of early intervention in the community, reducing the need for detox.
"We're seeing less people presenting to services with a new substance use of ketamine - so the education in schools, colleges and universities is actually working.
"But we are seeing an increase in people that have been using for a couple of years that we are going to continue to have to help and support."
With trends in drug use evolving, Moore said the challenge for both the third sector and the NHS was to adapt around the needs of clients, but that the involvement of those with lived experience had made a difference.
"I can see improvements now, but there have been some really difficult times where it felt like we were shouting in the dark."
Quelch said while research continued, the scale of the current ketamine problem was still unclear, as was the longer-term health implications.
"Anecdotally, relapse is a big problem in this group - we don't know the recoverability of their bodies, but we have seen that when people resume using ketamine after a period of abstinence, those harms appear a lot quicker than the first time around," he said.
However, Quelch added the work being done with peer support at Kaleidoscope was "really unique and impactful".
"There was a lack of judgement or stigmatisation - the peer element was really important and is something to learn from the Birchwood environment."
For Mark it has meant a focus on the future is possible. Like many we spoke to, he was adamant he wanted to give something back.
"I grew up thinking money was everything, but I get joy now from helping other people who are struggling. I was there once and I know how much it means to get someone to help you."

By Sinéad Carew and Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street with a 1% advance on Monday as investors returned to the chip sector and other AI-related stocks following last week's bruising selloff, while investors waited for key corporate earnings reports.
On Friday, the benchmark ‌S&P 500 and the Nasdaq had marked their biggest weekly declines since late June. Concerns that higher interest rates could curb investments in AI infrastructure ‌have been weighing on technology stocks, particularly chip companies and data center operators.
The selloff reflected mounting investor unease over how costly AI developments will be financed, a question that has increasingly pressured companies underpinning the ​US bull market, which recently marked its fourth anniversary.
Closing up 1.6% on Monday, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index snapped an eight-day losing streak in which it fell about 15.7% for its longest run of declines since October 2008.
"Rubber bands can only stretch so far in one direction before they snap and start reversing, and you finally saw that enough-is-enough moment in the semiconductors after Friday's close," said Michael James, managing director and equity sales trader at Rosenblatt Securities in Los Angeles.
"Nothing changed between Friday's close and this morning's open, other than nothing bad ‌happened over the weekend, and sentiment had gotten so negative ⁠that we were oversold to the point where a bounce was due," he added.
And with a lot of technology company earnings reports due out in coming days and weeks, James cautioned that the market is "far from out of the woods."
Social media company Meta, which ⁠finished down 0.5%, is due to report results on Wednesday along with electric vehicle company Tesla, while SpaceX is scheduled to report on Tuesday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 36.38 points, or 0.07%, to 51,966.03, the S&P 500 gained 31.29 points, or 0.41%, to 7,690.73 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 290.85 points, or 1.11%, to 26,430.89.
However, the market leaned massively on heavyweight stocks for ​its ​advance. Also during the session, the indexes had pulled away from their peaks for the day. One ​issue was that energy markets removed some earlier support as oil ‌prices fluctuated.
US crude oil futures reversed earlier losses to settle up 2.2% at $103.66 a barrel after attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on a Yemeni military training camp and renewed attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military facilities. [O/R]
Among the S&P 500's 11 major industry sectors, seven closed lower. Consumer discretionary was strongest with a 2.7% advance while technology was next, rising 1.2%. Defensive utilities, down 2%, and real estate, which lost 1.2%, were the biggest laggards among the sectors.
The biggest boosts to the consumer sector came from companies including Amazon.com, which finished up 5% after Morgan Stanley named the e-commerce and cloud computing firm its "top pick." Tesla provided the sector's second-biggest index point boost with a 3.8% ‌advance.
CoreWeave was at the center of last week's selloff after its shares plunged more than 25% on worries ​over a $50 billion debt load. Trading in the cloud computing provider ended the session down 0.4% after ​giving up early gains that appeared to be in response to Goldman ​Sachs' upgrade of the stock to "buy" from "neutral."
It was outperformed by peers Nebius, which added 2.9%, and Iren, which advanced 2.7%. Intel shares rallied ‌2.4% after J.P. Morgan upgraded the stock to "neutral" from "underweight."
Cleveland-Cliffs shares surged ​16% after the steelmaker surpassed analysts' estimates for ​its third-quarter profit.
Monday is the 39th anniversary of Black Monday, the 1987 crash that marked the biggest one-day decline in the history of the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.69-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 83 new highs and 265 new lows.
On the Nasdaq, 2,258 stocks ​rose and 2,647 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by ‌a 1.17-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 31 new highs and 361 new lows.
On ​US exchanges 15.27 billion shares changed hands compared with the 17.26 billion average for the last 20 sessions.

Hurricane Trudy will bring flood threat to the Southwest US
Trudy is off the Mexican coast, but its moisture will pour into the southwestern U.S. and will help fuel a multiday flood risk across seven states this week from California to Colorado.
A dip in the jet stream will also funnel in moisture from the Pacific as a strong low-pressure system moves into the region.
Wednesday: The highest risk of flooding on Wednesday covers much of Arizona and parts of New Mexico, as well as southern portions of Colorado and Utah.
There will be an abundance of moisture available to support heavy downpours and training storms. This means storms will produce heavy rain over the same areas for long periods of time. The Weather Prediction Center is forecasting rainfall rates as high as 2 inches per hour.
Some of the biggest concern will be the possibility of mudslides over recent burn scar areas as well as slow canyons and arroyos.
If you have plans to visit any of the national parks in the West this week, make sure you check the forecast daily and pay attention to any warnings or advisories issued.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
There is also a slight threat of severe weather on Wednesday for portions of Arizona and western New Mexico. Isolated strong wind and hail are the main threats, but a brief tornado is also possible.
Thursday: Moisture will continue to pump into the Southwest on Thursday, only enhancing the flood threat on already saturated soils.
Some forecast models are alluding to near record levels of moisture available for October in this region, which means there’s a great concern for flooding and the possibility that rainfall amounts could end up higher than currently forecast.
While the greatest risk for flooding moves out of California, it remains for much of Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah. This includes places like Las Vegas, Phoenix, Tucson and Albuquerque.
Right now, we are expecting as much as 3 inches of rain across portions of the Desert Southwest, which is more than enough for flash flooding in this region. Some isolated locations could see up to 5 inches.
And yes, we could even squeeze some snow out of this system for some of the higher elevations.
Parts of the Sierra and Rockies could see the first significant snow of the season. This could be a nice base for some of the ski resorts that were robbed of snow last winter.
While widespread snowfall totals will stay under 6 inches, we could see isolated peaks pick up a foot of snow.
Make sure you check back often, as the forecast could change. And don’t be caught off-guard if you are traveling through some of the higher elevations, as the rain could change to snow quickly.

articles.title_orig: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
articles.title_zh: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
articles.content_orig:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.
The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised.
In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped .
Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".
Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."
The new rules will give drivers:
Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.
Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.
With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.
The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.
The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.
The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.
But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament.
The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice".
The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.
Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".
But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.
The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

articles.title_orig: GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide. See affected products
articles.title_zh: GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide. See affected products
articles.content_orig:
How to Live Better, Longer
Federal inspectors who spent six days inside a Houston compounding pharmacy in August documented 14 problems with how it made sterile injectable drugs, including compounded GLP-1 weight-loss shots , according to an FDA inspection report . The pharmacy, Houston RX LLC, later recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide with niacinamide because of a lack of assurance of sterility.
The findings matter to anyone who buys compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide through a telehealth program, clinic, or med spa. Injectable drugs bypass the skin's natural barrier, so a contaminated vial can cause infection at the injection site or, less often, in the bloodstream. Patients usually cannot tell a safe vial from a compromised one by looking at it. Equipment that has not been depyrogenated, a process that removes fever-causing bacterial residues called endotoxins, can leave those residues behind even when no live germs remain.
The report, known as a Form 483, lists observations made during an inspection. The document states that these observations do not represent a final FDA determination about compliance, and the company can respond or correct them. MedicalDaily could not locate a public response from Houston RX.
Investigators inspected the pharmacy on Vantage Parkway East on six days between August 20 and August 28 and issued the report on the final day. The first observation is blunt: "Personnel performed aseptic manipulations with exposed hair or skin." Inspectors wrote that an operator working inside the ISO 5 hood, the cleanest workspace, had exposed skin on her forehead while stoppering freshly filled semaglutide-niacinamide vials.
Other observations describe the cleanroom air. Pressure readings from July 10 to August 21 between the buffer room and the less clean anteroom were all negative, a reversal that can let dirtier air drift toward sterile work. The report says lots made during that period were released.
Inspectors also wrote that on August 3 the pharmacy recovered microbial growth in the ISO 5 hood after filling a lot of tirzepatide-niacinamide. No investigation followed because the firm's action level was not appropriate, according to the FDA, and that lot was released and partially distributed.
The report adds that staff pressed stoppers into vials by hand, that vials were finished outside the clean area, and that beakers, stir bars and graduated cylinders used for sterile drugs were not sterilized or depyrogenated. A ceiling vent just outside the cleanroom had water stains and what appeared to be mold. On one inspection day, it was dripping condensate near the area where items headed into the cleanroom were wiped down.
Ingredients were another concern. Certificates for the tirzepatide and semaglutide active ingredients were marked for research and development only, as were certificates for other ingredients, and a sermorelin ingredient was labeled for scientific research use. The niacinamide used in all of the pharmacy's GLP-1 formulas met a dietary supplement standard rather than a pharmaceutical one, and several ingredients were not stored at their labeled temperatures.
According to FDA enforcement records summarized in the nonprofit MedShadow Foundation's roundup of recent compounded GLP-1 drug recalls , Houston RX began recalling 64 two-milliliter vials of tirzepatide-niacinamide 20 mg/2 mg per mL on September 25. The FDA classified it as a Class II recall, meaning use may cause temporary or medically reversible health problems, or that serious harm is unlikely. The pharmacy also recalled seven vials of compounded sermorelin, a growth hormone-releasing peptide, citing a lack of process control.
Recall details are posted in the FDA's weekly Enforcement Report database . Patients who use compounded tirzepatide should check the pharmacy name on the label or ask the prescriber which pharmacy filled the order.
Signs of a possible injection-site infection include spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus or pain that gets worse. Fever, chills, a racing heart, or confusion after an injection can signal a more serious infection and need urgent care. Patients should not stop a prescribed treatment without talking with a clinician, but they can ask for a replacement from a different source.
Side effects and product concerns can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program , and patients can keep the vial and packaging until they speak with a pharmacist.
Cost drives much of the demand. An October price survey by NexLife, a telehealth company that sells compounded GLP-1s, found a median all-in price of $222 a month for compounded tirzepatide across 14 online programs and $175 for compounded semaglutide across 16, according to its release on GlobeNewswire . Those figures were compiled by the company and have not been independently verified.
The trade-off is oversight. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and the agency's page on unapproved GLP-1 drugs reports 990 adverse event reports tied to compounded semaglutide and more than 730 tied to compounded tirzepatide as of May 31, 2026. The FDA says adverse events from compounded versions are likely underreported, though the reports alone do not prove the drugs caused the problems.
Houston RX is not the only pharmacy with recent sterility-related recalls. The same MedShadow roundup lists recalls of compounded GLP-1 products by Carolina Infusion in Ridgeland, South Carolina, and Apothecary Pharma in Cary, North Carolina.
Patients using compounded products can ask whether the pharmacy is licensed in their state, whether it has recent FDA inspection findings, and whether an FDA-approved version is covered by their insurance. Any further FDA action, such as a warning letter, would depend on the agency's review. For now, the recall notice and inspection report are the clearest public record of what inspectors found.
What did the FDA find at Houston RX?
An August inspection produced a Form 483 listing 14 observations, including exposed skin during sterile work, reversed cleanroom air pressure, microbial growth in a clean hood, unsterilized equipment, possible mold near the cleanroom, and research-grade ingredients.
Which products were recalled?
Houston RX recalled 64 vials of compounded tirzepatide-niacinamide 20 mg/2 mg per mL due to a lack of assurance of sterility and seven vials of compounded sermorelin due to a lack of process control. Both are Class II recalls.
How can I tell if my vial is affected?
Check the pharmacy name on the label and compare it with the FDA Enforcement Report. If you are unsure, ask your prescriber or the dispensing pharmacy.
No illnesses linked to the recalled vials have been publicly reported. The FDA has received more than 1,700 adverse event reports involving compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide overall, but those reports do not establish cause.
What symptoms should I watch for after an injection?
Watch for spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, or worsening pain at the injection site. Fever, chills, a fast heartbeat, or confusion need urgent medical care.
Should I stop my GLP-1 treatment?
Do not stop a prescribed medication on your own. Contact your prescriber to discuss a replacement from another pharmacy or an FDA-approved option.

articles.title_orig: Four AI Agents Have Slain Minecraft’s Ender Dragon
articles.title_zh: Four AI Agents Have Slain Minecraft’s Ender Dragon
articles.content_orig:
Google claims its newest AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, just beat Minecraft — no human help required.
In a research paper posted Oct. 15, Google DeepMind researchers said a team of four Gemini 4 Argon agents defeated the Ender Dragon, the game’s final boss. The agents started in a freshly generated survival world on Easy difficulty and were given a single goal: kill the dragon. It took them 27 hours and 14 minutes. Along the way, the AI players died 605 times, mostly to monsters.
The researchers say this is the first time AI agents have beaten Minecraft from start to finish using only standard tools, with no game-specific help built by humans. Researchers watched the run on a live dashboard and could have stepped in at any point, but they say they never needed to.
However, Google is upfront about the limits. The game ran on Easy, which meant that monster attacks dealt less damage to the AI players. Because the AI agents play the game through code rather than on a screen, they have access to information that a human player would not. For example, the AI agents knew what blocks were hidden behind other blocks, making the "mining" part of the game rather insignificant. Plus, given Gemini 4 Argon's training base, the AI agents knew the optimal strategies for playing the game.
It's impressive, but nowhere near what humans can do. The researchers note that the record for beating Minecraft in a random world is under seven minutes.
One may ask, why make an AI play Minecraft ? The researchers argue that the skills involved, like working as a team, bouncing back from mistakes, and sticking with a goal for more than a day, are the same ones AI agents need for real-world work. According to Google, the run costs about $520 in model usage at Argon’s introductory API price.
Making a frontier AI model play a video game is actually a common benchmark used by many companies when testing. The Pokémon games specifically have captured the zeitgeist in the AI industry for a while now, but Minecraft is now catching on too. As Google's research points out, two community projects have recently reported beating the dragon with AI , including one using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 .

articles.title_orig: Germany's Merz urges AI investment ahead of Nvidia deal
articles.title_zh: Germany's Merz urges AI investment ahead of Nvidia deal
articles.content_orig:
In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI.
Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.
The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies.
Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA.
The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI.
Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.”
Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition.
“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.”
Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience.
“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”
Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it.
“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”
Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included.
“If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.”
Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution.
“This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.”
Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI.
“I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.”
Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe.
NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs .
Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace.
Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare.
Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care.
Mirelo , a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen.
Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years.
Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory , advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%.
NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a record-breaking simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.

President Donald Trump has a major goal in mind to achieve before the end of his term, but it has nothing to do with policy.
Trump, 80, has always wanted to financially enrich himself above all else, his longtime biographer Michael Wolff said in the latest installment of his Substack, Howl .
But White House insiders have told him that the alleged total the president seeks is beyond any reasonable expectation.
âThe number people in the White House say, with due consideration and resigned acceptanceâTrump is Trump, after allâthat he wants to reach is $20 billion,â Wolff wrote. âAnd heâd probably like to put in place deals that, when he returns to Mar-a-Lago, can generate for the Trump family $100 million.â
Trump has made more than $2 billion during his second presidential term.
ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images
Wolff noted that Trump has already made, by many estimates, billions during his second administration.
The presidentâs financial disclosure , released in late June, revealed that he personally earned more than $1.4 billion in 2025 from cryptocurrency ventures alone.
Trump's wife Melania also launched her own memecoin, which failed miserably.
This included over $635 million in licensing fees from âCelebration Coinsâ and more than $525 million in proceeds from token sales by World Liberty Financialâthe cryptocurrency firm he founded with his sons.

A New York Times analysis gauged that Trump had âpulled in at least $2.2 billionâ in 2025, while Forbes estimated in September that he had become âan estimated $2.7 billion richer than when he won the 2024 election.â
Trumpâs love of money, Wolff writes, is what drives his relationship with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.
Late Friday, the president defied previous geopolitical strategy to waive sanctions on Russian oil, which many viewed as him cozying up to the oligarch .
Trump's infatuation with his dictator pal is no secret.

âPutin came to power in 1999,â Wolff wrote, after describing the fall of the Soviet Union and the subsequent âmoney grabâ in Russia. âControlling this new economy became his main political challenge.â

Trump has been pursuing Putin since the mid-1990s, Wolff wrote.
âThe presidency has certainly given him access to other irregular financial opportunities, but Trump is a creature of habit, and no opportunity has loomed as large in his mind as the money he might make in a partnership of equals with Vladimir Putin. And even not so equal,â he concluded.
Reached for comment, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the Daily Beast in a frequently recycled statement: âMichael Wolff is a professional scumbag and serial liar whose brain has been completely warped by his severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome.â

U.S. stock futures rose slightly on Monday night, following a mostly higher session on Wall Street as investors jumped back into tech names after a fierce sell-off last week.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 56 points higher, or 0.1%. S&P 500 futures climbed 0.1% along with Nasdaq-100 futures .
The S&P 500 climbed 0.4% in regular trading, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced more than 1%, with tech leading the charge. Nvidia added 1.4%, and Tesla jumped 3.8%. Alphabet shares advanced about 1%.
Tech last week suffered a rout that spilled over into the broader market, as concerns grew around companies borrowing too much money for their artificial intelligence build-outs.
"Improving moods regarding the prospects of modern technology have Wall Street breathing a sigh of relief as participants drop hedges, after the cost of volatility protection soared intraday on Friday, ahead of the intensifying selloff," wrote Jose Torres, senior economist at Interactive Brokers.
CoreWeave , which fell more than 25% last week, tried to recover some of that decline after a Goldman Sachs upgrade to buy. However, early gains fizzled and the stock closed slightly lower.
Investors on Tuesday will parse through a slew of corporate earnings. United Airlines is due to post after the bell, while General Motors is set to report before the open.
It's a busy week of earnings, with roughly 70 S&P 500 companies on deck to report results. Housing starts and pending home sales figures are also scheduled for release Tuesday.
AI stocks rallied on Monday, but CoreWeave closed slightly lower as investors remained skittish about its debt. Yields on Oracle debt also remained elevated as credit worries persist across the AI trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gained 1% on Monday. CoreWeave , the so-called neocloud company that led the sell-off last week, bounced around, hit a 52-week low and ultimately closed fractionally lower. Meanwhile, its bond yields remained high and its five-year credit default swaps were at distressed levels.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures traded 56 points higher, or 0.1%. S&P 500 futures climbed 0.1%. Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.2%.

articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.
Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.
Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.

Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.

Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.
Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.
Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.
He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."
The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X . She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.
"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.
For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.

On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.
TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.
Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.
TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.
However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.
“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”
AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.
“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.
Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote :
Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.
While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.
Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

Liquidity support buybacks are a standing Treasury tool rather than a policy signal: they target off-the-run securities in a defined sector, here the long end, and are funded out of regular issuance rather than net debt reduction. Operations of this kind have routinely been many times covered, as dealers use them to offload less liquid inventory, so heavy offer-to-accept ratios are the norm and not evidence of stress in the sector. The more informative figures are the concentration of the award, here only a small number of eligible CUSIPs purchased, which indicates where the cheapness and dealer positioning sit along that part of the curve, and the tail versus prevailing yields, which shows how much concession sellers had to give. For cash Treasuries the mechanism runs through the old-issue discount in the bought securities and, at the margin, the on-the-run versus off-the-run spread in the sector; effects on the outright long-end level have historically been negligible. The follow-ons are the regular buyback calendar, the share of the announced maximum actually taken across operations, and any shift in which securities are being offered most aggressively.

articles.title_orig: Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese
articles.title_zh: Homeland Security grants temporary deportation reprieve for more than 100K Ukrainians and Sudanese
articles.content_orig:
MIAMI — More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire Monday.
Temporary Protected Status was set to end Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time.” Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the U.S. covered by those temporary measures “retain protection.”
The Department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.
DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.
The decision Monday marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.
Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the U.S., described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches.”
It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for U.S. to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko added. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.
Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington think tank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.
“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them."
The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.
But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9. In that case, they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the U.S.
Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia .
Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.
The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive U.S. administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.
The decision Monday comes two weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.
The U.S. Congress created TPS in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife.
It allows people already in the country to remain and work, for renewable periods if the homeland security secretary determines conditions are unsafe for their return. But it doesn't give them a pathway to permanent residency.
Supporters say that using this tool protects people from being returned to dangerous situations and that uprooting people covered by TPS after years of living in the U.S. is cruel. Critics, especially in the Trump administration, say successive administrations have extended these protections for years regardless of what has happened in the home countries.
Federal rules say TPS is automatically extended for six months if the secretary doesn’t make a determination at least 60 days before the designation expires.
Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of Global Refuge, noted Ukraine and Sudan meet the legal conditions for TPS to be extended.
“It is not safe for these families to go home,” Vignarajah said.

articles.title_zh: Milan luxury shops close for fear of new unrest as government prepares to deploy troops
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrations over poor public services and rising costs spiralled over the weekend, with shops looted and property vandalised
Why are people protesting across Europe?
Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days ⁠of unrest that saw demonstrators ⁠clash with police, ​loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.
The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at ⁠a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.
“From words to action: 500 more ⁠troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.
Most stores in Milan’s Via ​Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior, had removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.
Several hundred hooded ‌protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.
Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who ‌faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.
“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.
As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.
Italian ⁠police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of ​those taken to police stations, 32 were ​arrested, including 23 minors and 13 ​foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.
